# Continuity and differentiability

Limits define continuity, while partial derivatives describe local change for functions of several variables.

## Exercises

### Continuity

::: {#exr-continuity-and-differentiability-given-does-limit-not-exist-why recommended="math" level="intermediate"}

Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be given by $$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & x > 0 \\
        -1 & x \leq 0 \end{cases}$$ For which $x \in \mathbb{R}$ does the limit $$\lim_{h \to 0} f(x + h)$$ *not* exist? Why?

:::

:::{#exr-continuity-and-differentiability-any-polynomial-continuous-theorem-properties-continuous}

Show that any polynomial $p:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, by using the theorem on properties of continuous functions.

:::

:::{#exr-continuity-and-differentiability-marsden-tromba-consider-function-function-defined}

(Marsden and Tromba) Consider the function $$f(x,y) = \frac{\sin(x^2 + y^2)}{x^2 + y^2}.$$ This function is defined on $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}$. Determine whether $f(x,y)$ approaches some value as $(x,y)\to(0,0)$. What is this value?

:::

::: {#exr-continuity-and-differentiability-marsden-tromba-does-exist-if-you recommended="math" level="intermediate"}

(Marsden and Tromba) Does $\lim_{(x,y)\to (0,0)} x^2/(x^2+y^2)$ exist? If you want, plotting the function can help.

:::

:::{#exr-continuity-and-differentiability-marsden-tromba-prove-argument}

(Marsden and Tromba) Prove that $\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} 2x^2y/(x^2+y^2) = 0$ using an $\epsilon$-$\delta$ argument.

:::

### Differentiability

:::{#exr-continuity-and-differentiability-compute-partial-derivatives}

Compute the partial derivatives of $$f(x,y) =  \frac{xy}{(x^2 + y^2)^{1/2}}.$$

:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="tutor"}

## Solutions

### Tutor note: Continuity

**Tutor note:** The concept of continuity is basic, so I recommend some of these exercises for everyone. I do not think the tutors need much preparation for them.

### Solution to @exr-continuity-and-differentiability-given-does-limit-not-exist-why {.unnumbered}

The limit does not exist at $x=0$. For every interval $]-\epsilon,\epsilon[$, $f$ maps into $\{-1,1\}$, which does not approach a single value.

### Solution to @exr-continuity-and-differentiability-any-polynomial-continuous-theorem-properties-continuous {.unnumbered}

The identity function $x \mapsto x$ is continuous. Since sums and products of continuous functions are continuous, every polynomial is continuous.

### Solution to @exr-continuity-and-differentiability-marsden-tromba-consider-function-function-defined {.unnumbered}

Use $\lim_{t\to0}\sin(t)/t=1$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $\eta>0$ such that $0<|t|<\eta$ implies $|\sin(t)/t-1|<\epsilon$. Set $\delta=\sqrt{\eta}$. If $0<\|\mathbf{u}\|<\delta$, then $0<\|\mathbf{u}\|^2<\eta$, so

$$
\left|\frac{\sin(\|\mathbf{u}\|^2)}{\|\mathbf{u}\|^2}-1\right|<\epsilon.
$$

Therefore the limit is $1$.

### Solution to @exr-continuity-and-differentiability-marsden-tromba-does-exist-if-you {.unnumbered}

A hint to give the students:

Consider the line $x=0$ and the line $y=0$.

The limit does not exist. Along $y=0$ the function equals $1$, while along $x=0$ it equals $0$.

### Solution to @exr-continuity-and-differentiability-marsden-tromba-prove-argument {.unnumbered}

We have $$|2 x^2 y/(x^2+y^2)| \leq |2 x^2 y/x^2| \leq 2|y|.$$ Thus, given $\epsilon > 0$, choose $\delta = \epsilon /2$. Then $0 < \|(x,y)-(0,0)\| = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} < \delta$ implies $|y|< \delta$, and so $|f(x,y) -0| < 2\delta < \epsilon$.

### Tutor note: Differentiability

**Tutor note:** The source contains only one exercise on differentiability; more exercises may be added later.

### Solution to @exr-continuity-and-differentiability-compute-partial-derivatives {.unnumbered}

For $(x,y)\neq(0,0)$, write $v=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}$. The quotient and chain rules give

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}
=\frac{yv-xy(x/v)}{v^2}
=\frac{y^3}{(x^2+y^2)^{3/2}},
$$

and, by symmetry,

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}
=\frac{x^3}{(x^2+y^2)^{3/2}}.
$$

:::
